splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans. The Supreme Court resolved this split.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected before the statutory measurement date, providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current data in their calculations.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the court-ordered supervision period beyond the judgment's specified term when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to find violations and revoke release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding, and the term expires as originally set absent explicit statutory authorization for tolling.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1), which categorically bars claims previously presented, when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any prior claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like mail-in ballot receipt deadlines. The split affects how easily candidates can challenge election rules before an election, with significant implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting procedures absent a concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps agency deference in the criminal sentencing context. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit panel held that agency deference trumps lenity. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron, casting further doubt on strong deference in criminal cases.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's interpretations when a Guidelines provision is ambiguous in a criminal context.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity when the Commission's interpretation is reasonable, even in criminal cases.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in the career-offender guideline is entitled to deference after Kisor narrowed agency-deference doctrine. Some circuits defer to the commentary; others hold the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (all three criminal-history criteria must be met to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision. This determines whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on jurisdiction.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled or whether a state-law controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on the federal schedule.

positions.label: State scheduling suffices
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction counts as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines even if the substance is not controlled under the federal CSA, because the guideline text references state law offenses without a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes, alone or in combination with other factors, can never constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons. Others, relying on the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendments to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), allow courts to consider them. This split affects prisoners serving stacked § 924(c) sentences and others whose sentences would be lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's contrary policy statement exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, particularly under the Commission's amended policy statement at § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violating the conditions of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be justified solely on the basis of the original offense and other § 3553(a) factors.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation that are expressly based on punishing the defendant for the violations themselves. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis permits courts to punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits limit the revocation sentence to considerations related to the original offense.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations at revocation, in addition to considering the original offense.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is not the purpose of revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of trust inherent in the original offense and not on punishing the specific violations of supervised release conditions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may bring a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges to conditions of confinement or whether prisoners may also bring civil rights claims. This split has evolved over decades and affects federal prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits, prerelease custody, and other conditions of confinement.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions that could affect the duration of confinement, including First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody, must be brought through habeas corpus rather than civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights claims to challenge conditions of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment, even when habeas may also be available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the applicable time limit to appeal a Hyde Amendment order (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 60-day civil appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because it is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case and is thus subject to the shorter criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits have not uniformly resolved whether orders denying motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review, as delayed review risks irreversible disclosure.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be effectively vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of sealing orders generally is not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as privacy interests can be adequately protected through other means.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether property appreciation occurring between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate; the dissent noted this creates a circuit split with courts holding the appreciation belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's structure, legislative history, and policy of encouraging good-faith conversions.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, affecting hospitality, retail, and service industries. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the disagreement and clarify liability and damages standards. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing discrimination liability in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard requiring stronger proof of discriminatory intent or treatment in business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
